speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smoking is the primary cause of lung cancer and is also a risk factor for other types of cancer, such as cancers of the mouth, upper throat, oesophagus, bowel and bladder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smoking is also a risk factor for many major chronic diseases, such as high blood pressure, chronic lung diseases, heart disease and stroke.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Tobacco itself contains more than 60 chemicals, including nicotine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Once addiction sets in, many smokers find it difficult to quit even though they might want to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Worldwide, tobacco is the cause of approximately six million deaths annually.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: More than five million of those deaths are a result of direct tobacco use, while more than 600,000 are the result of exposure to second-hand smoke.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many deaths due to tobacco use are preventable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smoking is the second highest risk factor that contributes to the burden of disease in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We did this by being aggressive in our tobacco control measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We introduced progressively stricter restrictions on smoking advertisements, banned the use and possession of tobacco by minors under 18, introduced mandatory graphic health warnings and banned misleading descriptors, such as "mild" or "light".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have tightened up our tobacco control measures in the past two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In November 2014, we introduced the ban on shisha or water pipe tobacco.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In December last year, we banned emerging tobacco products not currently in the Singapore market, such as smokeless cigarettes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On 1 August this year, the ban will be extended to products available here, such as snuff and gutkha.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, MOH will be using the opportunity to further streamline our tobacco control measures and address new regulatory challenges posed by the tobacco industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, let me elaborate on the point-of-sale display ban.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ban on point-of-sale display of tobacco products is a continuation of our tobacco control efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The aim is to, ultimately, de-normalise tobacco use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Other countries, such as Australia, Canada, Iceland, New Zealand, Thailand and the UK, have successfully introduced a point-of-sale display ban.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The new section 12A in clause 14 of the Bill will introduce the prohibition on the display of tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will apply to all tobacco products, including cigars, beedies, "ang hoon" and others, in addition to cigarettes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: General tobacco retailers will be required to use storage devices to keep tobacco products out of the direct line of sight of customers and the public within their premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They may choose different methods to comply with the ban, so long as the storage unit is self-closing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Options include using gravity flaps, vertical blinds, curtains or automated sliding/closing doors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As per current requirements, the storage unit has to be plain and without design, sound or lighting decorations, as these could draw attention to the storage units and be used as a form of advertising.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Specialist tobacconists serve a niche market, as they sell primarily cigars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Unlike customers of general retailers, who may be shopping for other products, most customers who step into a specialist tobacconist shop have already made up their mind to buy tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hence, for such shops, we will focus on limiting the advertising impact from outside the shops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Regulations will be crafted to allow specialist tobacconists to display their products within their premises, so long as the products are not visible from outside the premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Following feedback and appeals, general tobacco retailers will be allowed to use a text-only price list to facilitate communications with customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Display of the price list is allowed only upon customers' request and its appearance will be prescribed by MOH.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is provided for in the new section 3(1A) in clause 4 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have engaged tobacco retailers extensively since 2014 and briefed them on the requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Tobacco retailers will be given a one-year grace period before the point-of-sale display ban takes effect.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Globally, there has been a marked increase in the popularity of electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS), also known as e-cigarettes, especially among young people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Studies show that high school students who use ENDS are more likely to move on to smoke cigarettes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To protect public health, Singapore has pre-emptively banned the import, distribution and sale of ENDS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: ENDS are banned under the existing Act as imitation tobacco products that are designed to resemble existing tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Earlier models of ENDS looked like traditional cigarettes, to appeal to smokers or would-be smokers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, newer varieties of ENDS do not necessarily look like cigarettes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They target not just current smokers, but also seek to expand market demand, especially among youth and women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 18 of the Bill repeals and re-enacts section 16 of the Act to make it clear that the existing ban on the importation, distribution and sale of imitation tobacco products also includes products that may be used in such a way as to mimic the act of smoking, even though they may not necessarily physically resemble cigarettes or other tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With the increasing popularity of ENDS, there is a need to control the advertising of such products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 4 extends the existing prohibition on advertisements for tobacco products to imitation tobacco products and corresponding amendments will be made to sections 6, 7 and 8 of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With expansion of online access, there is increasing use of the Internet for tobacco advertising and commerce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As part of the global public health community, Singapore should ensure that our existing prohibitions on tobacco advertising and promotion are comprehensive and cover online advertising and promotion originating from Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is in compliance with the World Health Organization's Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, to which Singapore is a signatory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These include advertisements originating from Singapore, even if targeted at a foreign audience, as well as advertisements originating from outside Singapore that are accessible by persons physically in Singapore and published by a Singapore-connected person.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A "Singapore-connected person" is defined in clause 2 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The amended section 3 also prohibits Internet advertisements that provide a facility to the person accessing these advertisements to buy tobacco products or imitation tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 9 amends section 9 to prohibit tobacco product sales promotions that originate from Singapore, even if targeted at persons outside Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Sales promotional schemes have evolved over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides the changes outlined above, we also took the opportunity to make a number of additional amendments to the Act to be in line with the latest legal policy developments, improve clarity, and enhance its implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some of these are as follows: Clause 12 amends the wording of section 11 to improve clarity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Authorised officers may seize the tobacco products if an offence is committed under section 11(1).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 15 allows the Health Sciences Authority to specify the visual characteristics of the "No sale to minors" sign used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The existing ban on sale of tobacco products via vending machines will now be covered under the amended section 18.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, a supermarket may only have one point of sale for tobacco products, which is already the current practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Minister will be empowered to make regulations to give effect to these licensing requirements, as provided for in clause 31.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, the Minister will be able to make regulations to specify the fees to be paid by tobacco wholesalers and retailers and the length of time for which the licences are granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 24 provides that Police officers and authorised officers are empowered to ask a suspect to produce identification, search his bags and require him to reveal the contents of his pockets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is necessary to prevent suspects from concealing evidence in their bags or pockets from enforcement officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As a safeguard, enforcement officers have been trained to follow standard operating procedures strictly and regularly undergo refresher training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: No physical search of the body is involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 25 enhances the powers of investigations, by allowing the Chief Executive, HSA, and authorised officers to require relevant information to be furnished in writing, for the purposes of investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clause 26 amends section 26 to empower the Chief Executive and authorised officers to inspect and seize electronic documents and materials, computers or other relevant equipment in which evidence may be stored and to request that access codes or passwords be provided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The clause also extends existing search powers of premises to include conveyances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It will be an offence to wilfully fail to comply with a requirement made under the amended section 26.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clauses 28 and 29 extend the scope of powers of forfeiture to include any imitation tobacco product, document, material or article and empower the Chief Executive to give directions on the disposal of forfeited items seized under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The amendments here take into account the other changes in this Bill, as well as the changing enforcement landscape, and are scoped to allow HSA to continue exercising its functions under the Act effectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Similar powers of seizure are provided for in the Health Products Act and the Sale of Food Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Though we are fortunate that smoking prevalence in Singapore has remained relatively low compared to many other countries, we must not be complacent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also know the industry aggressively markets their products to youth, so as to hook them from an early age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As such, we must continue and, in fact, step up our efforts to protect the public from the advertising effects of tobacco and introduce new measures to enable us to keep pace with the rapid changes in the industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From a social viewpoint, tobacco use impinges on other peoples' lives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From an economic standpoint, the health problems created impose a financial burden on all taxpayers – you, me and everybody.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This does not include the emotional and mental suffering of the victims and families who lose their loved ones due to smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have, as part of our anti-smoking campaign, required cigarette packs to carry graphic images and warnings since 2004.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This was recommended as part of WHO's Tobacco Free Initiative.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Such graphic warnings were found to be generally effective in creating awareness and motivating people to quit smoking, according to a study by the Harvard School of Public Health.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, a survey done in 2013 showed that many smokers in Singapore were undeterred by the graphic warnings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A similar sentiment was echoed by a British study held in the same year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we need to review policies regularly and explore new solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many tobacco companies and retailers rely on point-of-sale displays to compensate for the inability to advertise tobacco sales in many countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In some local convenience stores, cigarette packages dominate the most eye-catching display wall.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The display takes a premium spot, for example, next to the cashier's counter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In several countries, the UK, Canada, Thailand, Australia, New Zealand among others, such displays are banned.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Centre for Tobacco Control Research at the University of Stirling said 46% of UK teenagers were aware of the displays and those who intended to smoke were more likely to recall brands they had seen at the point of sale.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Research by the Centre for Behavioural Research in Cancer in Australia and Stanford University in the US confirmed this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A study of 25,000 young people in New Zealand found that children exposed to displays were almost three times more likely to smoke.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Research in Australia and the US shed light on the rationale: point-of-sale-display advertising of cigarettes normalises tobacco use for children and creates a perception that tobacco is easily obtainable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To further drive home the point, RAND Corporation did a one-of-a-kind laboratory replica of a convenience store to examine whether limiting displays of tobacco products in retail outlets could reduce the intention of young people to begin smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Point-of-sale display is a common sales promotion tactic.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe many of us can recount a time when we bought something on impulse at the cashier, simply because seeing it stimulated a desire for it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is already a blanket ban on advertising and promotion of tobacco products in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It only makes sense to extend the ban to point-of-sale displays.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I pledge my full support for the ban on tobacco displays.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By the same logic, it seems ideal to prohibit Internet advertising, especially as our youths spend more and more time on the Internet.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Online shopping is fast growing and last year, a news report indicated that people were hawking banned e-smoking devices online.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I have to caution against the possible limitations of this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When there is too little of something, it becomes a novelty, a taboo, an object of curiosity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Consider drugs and marijuana, they are never openly sold, yet people fall prey to it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just recently, "Ah Boys to Men" actor Noah Yap was sentenced to nine months detention for taking cannabis.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the World Wide Web is too extensive to police.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just do a search and you will find a number of smoking and drug-use advocacy pages on Facebook with thousands of followers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are even web articles dedicated to paparazzi shots of celebrities smoking, glamorising smoking in a perfectly legal way.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, there is a limit to the effect of banning point-of-sale displays and Internet advertising.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I recall a news report that interviewed a smoker who had been smoking since he was 15.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "I do not need to see the pack to crave a cigarette.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What matters most is the smell." When adults smoke, children and teens see them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They walk by and they whiff the smoke.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, we must invest more resources in continued public awareness and outreach efforts, both for youths and adults.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Smoke-free zones in public spaces can also reduce the visual and nasal temptation of cigarettes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, we have piloted designated smoking points at one zone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are smokers who use them though there are still some smokers who smoke outside them, but I believe that, through social conditioning, we can eventually be like Japan, where most smokers voluntarily smoke at designated spaces.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, I hope to see a wider adoption of Designated Smoking Points to minimise exposure of non-smokers to second-hand smoke that causes cancer, heart disease, lung disease and childhood illnesses, including cot death and asthma.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We must also create an environment that is more supportive and encouraging for potential quitters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When we piloted the Designated Smoking Points in my constituency, we also had Blue Ribbon Ambassadors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These ambassadors would not only encourage smokers to smoke in the designated smoking points, but also advise them on how to quit smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we can eventually pool together more resources to turn it into a nation-wide effort.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are striving to be a more compassionate society and, in our good intentions to combat the harmful effects of smoking, we must not make smokers feel alienated and criminalised.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I posted on my Facebook page about me speaking on this tobacco Bill and one of my residents messaged me, she told me that she started smoking at age 15.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And she says that you can increase the price of cigarettes, you can put it in different packaging, you can show all the eerie, ugly pictures of the smokers; it will not deter them from smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That gave her the hope and the desire and the motivation to quit smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, she started to quit smoking but she said she failed many times.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And now I ask her how old she is now, she said she is 32, happily married with a daughter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to ask for more such encouragement for those smokers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, we need to have more educational talks in schools to deter people from even starting to smoke and perhaps show them how to do so, how to have stress management because many of them say that they picked up smoking because of the stress in school.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, introduce to them meditation, introduce them to sports and, for those already smoking, there is another set of education – to give them hope and chance to reverse their lungs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having said much on the hazards of tobacco smoking, I would like to briefly wrap up by asking for help to small retailers who sell cigarettes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What substitute can they sell in place of cigarettes to generate income?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As part of our commitment to help small businesses, I hope the Ministry will be able to look into the situations of these small shops.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore has been actively bringing down the smoking rate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Prohibiting shops from displaying tobacco products and banning online tobacco advertisements will minimise the temptation to the young and, hopefully, can reduce the smoking rate effectively.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, the effect of these measures can still be limited as young people can easily see or smell adult smoking on the street.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This may even give them the impression that smoking is a sign of adulthood, enticing them to try smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I suggest that we should build more Designated Smoking Points that are far away from schools and crowded areas so as to reduce the temptation to youngsters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we must pay more attention to encouraging and helping smokers to quit smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the authorities can look into how to help these small shops transform.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I look after patients with cancer, including smoking-related cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have sat by the bedside of patients suffering from advanced lung cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have seen what happens when a life is cut short and dies because of smoking.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it has been known in the scientific community even before Singapore's Independence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of the first studies was actually done in the UK by British doctor, Sir Richard Doll, published in 1950.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Around the world, there has been plenty of research on this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Harvard Medical School recently has also found that there is no safe minimum level of tobacco use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know that, today, among all cancers in Singapore, lung cancer is the number two killer among male cancer patients and lung cancer is the number three killer among female cancer patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know that smoking-related diseases are among the top killers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would you want such a substance on sale in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or would you want to keep Singaporeans and our children safe from it?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It hurts those around the smoker: co-workers, family members and, especially, young children – who are put at higher risk of asthma, lung infections and, in some cases, the Sudden Infant Death Syndrome.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Smoking can also make the living environment quite unpleasant for neighbours.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A number of my Clementi residents have shared these concerns with me.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, why is tobacco still around in Singapore, despite these harms?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Tobacco has been around for a long time in the world and in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: An addictive chemical, once entrenched, is very hard to roll back – no matter the harmful consequences, the poisonous effects of the substance on the consumer, their family and society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This has deep lessons for our efforts in other Ministries, especially regarding drug control, but, today, I will focus on tobacco.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, how might one roll back the presence of tobacco in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Of those who have already started smoking, they find it very, very difficult to quit.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I have sympathy for how difficult it can be for a smoker to quit.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember a patient who could not stop smoking even though he had been diagnosed with lung cancer, even though he had young children at home breathing his second-hand smoke.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He could not bring himself to stop because he was addicted.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, while it is important to help existing smokers to quit, the greatest battle is upstream: for the hearts and minds and help of our children and youth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must make sure they never start smoking in the first place.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I call upon MOH to go even further and consider such a proposal.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because a Tobacco-Free Generation policy does not disadvantage existing smokers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of them are still battling their addiction.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They would still be able to purchase cigarettes, subject to the prevailing laws and regulations, even as they try to quit.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, over time, there would be fewer smokers and less harm caused by second-hand smoke.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The original Tobacco-Free Generation campaigns focused on the Year 2000.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The children of the year 2000 will be 16 years old this year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In two more years, they will be 18 years old.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Old enough to start thinking about buying cigarettes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some may even have started smoking because of peer pressure and illegal cigarettes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is not too late to raise the minimum legal age further.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But even better still, Mdm Speaker, if we implement a Tobacco-Free Generation policy, either way, this will help us build towards a Tobacco-Free, smoke-free, SG100 and a healthier future for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: All these and more have been linked to smoking and exposure to tobacco smoke.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That is, practically, the whole body's organs and systems!

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Smoking causes more deaths annually than HIV/AIDs; plus illegal drug use; plus alcohol use; plus motor vehicle accidents; plus firearms-related injuries, all put together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Tobacco is the single greatest cause of preventable death globally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, the reason why this Bill is critical for us and for Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It will also help us push the envelope further after being the first ASEAN country to ban tobacco advertisements in 1971 – that is, very early on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, the first ASEAN country to introduce graphic pictures to warn of the dangers of smoking on cigarette packs in 2003; and also being a party to the WHO Framework Convention in Tobacco Control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I also want to share on the proposal and concept of tobacco-free generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is a worldwide movement and it is also quite active in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have been a part of this movement, as with several other Members and we have many students, youths and members of the public who have come forward as ambassadors to the messaging and movement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This relates to the banning of the provision of tobacco to any citizen born after a specific year and the year 2000 has been chosen and proposed as it is easy to remember.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are some jurisdictions that have taken this up more formally, even for debate at their parliamentary levels and in different legislatures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, I have the following clarifications to make: first, are there any tobacconist or such similar facilities or stores that we have in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If we do, as they are specific niche theme facilities, how will we be managing and regulating them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Two, for duty free outlets, how will the change be implemented?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is mentioned that they will be regulated later, thus what kind of timeline are we looking at?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are there any chances that we could shorten this grace period?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, on the text-only price listing, can the Minister elaborate what exactly can it contain?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fifth, can the Minister also share with us or summarise the application of the Bill in cyber space because it is not uncommon that for every web page that we visit at the peripheral, there are always advertisements related to smoking, and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   I fully support this Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Each year, our Malay community occupies the top position in the national statistics on smoking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must, as a community, try our very best to reduce this figure further, because this is associated with our health and the lives of our future generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our Malay community also has poor health statistics, and smoking is linked to many chronic diseases that affect us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: To our young people, please do not associate smoking with the coming of age or the rites of passage, or as a symbol of adulthood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, we must put together a better and stronger effort to improve and reduce these figures significantly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Everyone, every citizen, every family member plays a very critical role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are also voluntary bodies that conduct many programmes to kick the smoking habit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The upcoming Ramadan month this year can be used as the starting point for you to stop smoking completely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As the saying goes: "Where there is a will, there is a way." So, let us work together with everyone to ensure better health for all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Madam, this Bill is about society's stand against cigarette smoking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is a strong trend noted worldwide, for those who start smoking as teenagers, they do go on to become adult and long-term tobacco users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We in this House can take the step to break the vicious cycle and we must do it and do it now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a former smoker, I fully support the controls and measures that will be put in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On 12 October 2013, I took my last puff after smoking for 17 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have not smoked since and I do not intend to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I tried without success to reduce my smoking for many years but I ultimately decided that "cold turkey" was the best way to quit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I did play cheat a little as I quit smoking when I was at a conference in Disneyland.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was a place I knew did not sell cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was there for a week and, as such, it made it harder for me to get a cigarette in case I gave in to my cravings, which were quite severe during the first week of quitting.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was hard to quit, the nicotine withdrawal symptoms were terrible and I was a grouchy smurf for quite a while.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it was worth it and I feel healthier now, my family members benefit and are healthier as well, and I save loads of money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there was one thing I remembered about the quitting process, it was that I did my very best to avoid places selling cigarettes, which was actually very difficult or impossible at times as I had to avoid 7-Elevens, coffee shops and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every time I saw a cigarette packet, it was tempting and my cravings shot up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will not only help people who are trying to quit but also possibly reduce the number of people who are enticed to start smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments to curb tobacco product advertisements are also crucial in our fight to lower smoking rates in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the goal of advertisements is to make you buy what you do not want to buy and we need to make sure people are not driven or tempted, either subconsciously or consciously, into smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There was previous discussion about raising the minimum smoking age to 21 years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify why this proposal was not included in this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support this Bill but I do have one concern with regard to the amended section 26(1)(b) and (c) which allows the Chief Executive or an authorised officer to, at any time and without warrant, enter and search any premise, stop, board and search any conveyance that the Chief Executive or authorised officer reasonably suspects is being used for or in connection with the commission of an offence under this Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify why a warrant is not required and what safeguards will be put in place to ensure that there will be no abuse of this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am especially concerned that even authorised officers are allowed to do this, to search without a warrant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, ultimately, as always, we need to go beyond legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Controlling the advertisement and sale of tobacco and increased enforcement efforts can help, and probably have helped, to reduce the smoking rates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I believe that public education is the long-term solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I remember when I was young, there was a campaign with the slogan, "One puff and you are hooked." The distinct image of a smoker with a fishing hook in his mouth is still fresh in my memory.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think we need to change the narrative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While that had the desired effect of educating the public on the dangers and addictive nature of cigarettes, it also gave a fatalistic view of smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has mentioned earlier with her resident's story, I think many felt that since they are already smoking and it is so hard to quit, they might as well just continue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, while we focus on efforts to ensure that people do not start smoking, let us also see how we can intensify our efforts to encourage more smokers to quit, to show them that it is possible to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The last big public campaign that was launched was the "I Quit" campaign in 2011.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry expand this campaign this year, which will be held in May?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we think out of the box to launch more campaigns that will help us to reach our aim of getting smoking rates down to 12% by 2020?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are many things we can learn from other successful "quit smoking" campaigns around the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One such example is the "Tips from Former Smokers" Campaign by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in the USA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the main strategies of the campaign was to focus on real people and stories on how smoking has affected their lives and how they managed to quit smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While it is true that everyone knows smoking is bad for health, the personal stories shared in this campaign were compelling and communicated in a very human way that smoking causes immediate damage to your body and that this damage can happen at a young age and can be severe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It sparked a national conversation and encouraged non-smokers to speak to their loved ones who smoke.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think we are all aware of the health risks to smokers and those exposed to smoke.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Smoking is a significant contributor to disease burden.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of us have spoken and expressed concern about the increasing healthcare expenditure by the Government.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By the simple act of eliminating smoking, this would have a significant impact on reducing healthcare utilisation and also healthcare expenditure in many countries, including our own.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore has made much progress in controlling smoking rates and now boasts one of the lowest smoking rates in the world.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But more can be done and there are areas of concern.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most smokers also pick up the habit in their youth and smoking cessation remains a challenge to most smokers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I feel that this amendment is both timely and forward-looking.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the strict regulation and restriction of tobacco-related products in many countries, tobacco companies have been focusing their marketing efforts at the points of sale.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And many studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of such a strategy in enticing new smokers and also making it harder for smokers to quit.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, instituting a point-of-sale display ban has been shown to be effective in both reducing smoking initiation and also helping smoking cessation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think many of us have experienced this.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When we go for a meal in a shopping mall, in a supermarket queue waiting to pay for our purchases, or at the petrol kiosk waiting to pay for our petrol, we end up purchasing things that we did not actually think we were going to purchase that were just available and attractively displayed at the counter.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This phenomenon of impulse buying is well recognised by retailers and has been exploited by most retailers, including cigarette companies.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A study conducted a few years ago by researchers at Johns Hopkins found that, in the US, as much as 11.2% of cigarette buyers were impulse buyers and the most likely impulse buyers were the young between 18 and 24 years old and also those who were occasional smokers and, finally, those who were trying to quit.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And close to a third of respondents confirmed that point-of-sale displays made quitting harder for them.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides Singapore, a few other countries have instituted point-of-sale display bans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Iceland was the first to do so, followed by several other countries – Thailand, Ireland, Norway, Finland, Canada and Australia.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And Singapore will be the next on the list.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Studies conducted in some of these countries since the ban have clearly demonstrated a marked reduction in consumer exposure to tobacco products, as well as a significant reduction in impulse buying.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A review of 20 scientific studies have also overwhelmingly confirmed the association between point-of-sale displays and smoking promotion and susceptibility.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A recent meta-analysis, which is a study that reviews the evidence provided by other well-regarded studies, was published in January this year and it looked specifically at the relationship between point-of-sale displays and smoking rates and susceptibility in the young and adolescents.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this study concluded that "legislation banning tobacco point-of-sale promotion will effectively reduce smoking amongst young people." I think it is reassuring that this amendment to the TCASA will spell the end of the Tobacco Power Wall in Singapore and also tighten regulations pertaining to online advertising and marketing and also close loopholes regarding imitation tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have two further issues to raise, which I hope the Ministry will be able to consider.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, it is with regard to the minimum age at which persons can use or purchase tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is good evidence that such a move will further reduce smoking initiation rates and there appears to be broad support from the public for such a move, as indicated by the findings of the recent public consultations for this amendment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The World Health Organization has also stated, based on prevailing evidence, that people who do not begin smoking before the age of 21 are unlikely to become chronic smokers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that the Ministry is already studying this and I call upon the Ministry to expedite this move.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Australia was the first jurisdiction to have done so and the impact thus far has been encouraging and several other countries have also indicated that similar legislation is in progress.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is strong opposition to such legislation from tobacco companies and some of them are even bringing lawsuits against governments, but I think this is just another indication that standard packaging would further reduce smoking initiation and accelerate smoking cessation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Clearly, all of us have been touched by the issue of smoking at some point in our lives, either personally or professionally.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng has shared how, as a medical oncologist, he had witnessed first-hand the damage wrought on his patients by tobacco.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef has pointed out the diseases caused by tobacco – it seems as if almost every organ in the body can be affected by tobacco use!

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng provided personal insights on how difficult it can be to quit smoking and how he tried to avoid point-of-sale displays of cigarettes while quitting.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I must commend him for being creative in quitting smoking by going "cold turkey" in Disneyland.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During my engagement session with tobacco retailers in December 2015, one comment made stayed with me for a long time.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A retailer told me that even though he sold tobacco, he did not want his own children to smoke!

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: He acknowledged that tobacco could cause addiction among his customers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is why we need to continue to strengthen our tobacco control measures and provide a supportive environment for smokers to quit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We need to make sure that our youth do not pick up the habit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We want to bring smoking rates down even more.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The point-of-sale display ban plays a part in fulfilling these objectives.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the point-of-sale display ban, I had earlier described the requirements for general tobacco retailers to keep their tobacco products out of sight of customers and the public within their premises.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I also said that specialist tobacconists are required to keep tobacco products out of sight from outside their premises because these specialist tobacconists usually sell mainly cigars and, perhaps, alcohol.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To do this, they can completely make their store windows opaque, use curtains or any other method that achieves the same effect.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about duty-free retailers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Unlike general tobacco retailers, duty-free retailers at Changi Airport serve mostly tourists and overseas passengers who are departing Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Like specialist tobacconists, the requirements will be slightly different from those for general tobacco retailers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Duty-free retailers at seaports may place their tobacco products within a specified "tobacco area" of the premises, but the tobacco products should not be visible from outside this area.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Alternatively, they may follow the requirements for general tobacco retailers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: DFS Galleria at Scotts is classified as a general tobacco retailer and will be required to comply with the requirements for general tobacco retailers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked what the price list will look like.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The appearance of the price list will be prescribed by MOH.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It should be in text, printed on white A4 paper and contain only the necessary information on the product, such as brand and variant, price barcode and stock number.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As not all customers are literate in English, we will permit the price list to be published in each of the four official languages.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But this is limited to one price list per official language.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef recommends that we shorten the grace period of one year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am pleased to see her enthusiastic support for the ban.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Much as it would be ideal to implement the ban as soon as possible, the reality is that tobacco retailers, especially the smaller shops, will need time to make the necessary adjustments to their existing store set-up.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The grace period also gives them time to diversify their business models away from the sale of tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, MOH certainly encourages retailers to comply early with the requirements of the ban.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah expressed concern that tobacco retailers, especially the smaller businesses, would be affected financially by this ban.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have conducted engagement sessions with small retailers since 2014 to help them prepare for the ban.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The ban applies to all general tobacco retailers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As such, no tobacco retailer will lose out to another.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Like all our tobacco control measures, the intended effect is to decrease the overall demand for cigarettes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But as this will likely not be an immediate development, small retailers can use this grace period and beyond to start shifting their business models away from dependence on selling tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They may also consider changing their business practices to increase their productivity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members have suggested additional ways to enhance tobacco control, especially measures to prevent youths from picking up smoking and to help smokers quit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu had suggested that we follow in Australia's footsteps and quickly move to introduce standardised packaging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Emerging data from Australia shows that standardised packaging reduces the attractiveness of the tobacco products and makes the health warnings more prominent and effective.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are early indications that it reduces smoking prevalence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have been studying and are closely monitoring international developments on standardised packaging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In May this year, France, the UK and the Republic of Ireland will start to implement standardised packaging as well.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The decision on whether or not to proceed with standardised packaging will be based on public health considerations and we will also ensure that any measure, if introduced, will be designed in a manner consistent with our international obligations, including those relating to intellectual property rights.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I fully agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef that tobacco control is best managed upstream – that is, we win the hearts and minds of our children and youths to prevent them from getting addicted in the first place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: That is why Health Promotion Board (HPB) works with MOE and Institutes of Higher Learning to incorporate anti-tobacco messages into the curriculum, so as to raise awareness about the benefits of a tobacco-free lifestyle, dispel the misconceptions about smoking and equip youths with life skills to refuse cigarette offers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I also applaud efforts by passionate volunteers to get our youths to pledge to be a tobacco-free generation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Going beyond promotional measures, both Dr Tan Wu Meng and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef had proposed that we could also introduce a cohort ban on smoking, by banning sales of tobacco to Singaporeans born from the year 2000 or another specified year onwards.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH is familiar with this proposal and has given it a lot of thought.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our concerns are the significant practical difficulties and risks in implementing and enforcing such a ban and it may not result in the desired reduction in smoking rates.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Such a cohort ban would be easy to circumvent and enforcement is going to be challenging and likely to be resource-intensive.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: An effective ban would also require laws to penalise persons not subject to the ban who supply tobacco products to the affected cohort.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, a person affected by the ban could buy cigarettes overseas, or get an older relative or friend unaffected by the ban to buy cigarettes for them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In such a situation, we would have to penalise the person providing the cigarettes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But we are aware that this idea is being pursued in Tasmania, Australia, through a Private Member's Bill and we will monitor its development.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked why MOH had not included raising the minimum legal age for buying tobacco and smoking in this current set of amendments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah made a similar call for MOH to raise the minimum legal age.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Raising the minimum legal age to 21 years is a relatively new measure in jurisdictions that have implemented it, such as Hawaii and New York City.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, we would need to carefully study their experiences and see if this would be appropriate in our local context.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH agrees with Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Louis Ng and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that public education efforts and support for smokers to quit smoking complement legislative measures.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They are key elements of our multi-pronged approach towards tobacco control.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng made a call to intensify efforts to encourage more smokers to quit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Quitting can be perceived as a rather challenging journey by smokers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, HPB introduced the "I Quit 28 Day Countdown" in 2013, to get smokers to quit by breaking down the quit journey into daily, small actionable steps.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah said, by the end of 28 days, the body will be back to normal as before they started smoking.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is based on findings that smokers who stay smoke-free for 28 days are five times more likely to quit smoking for good.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Like the "Tips from Former Smokers" campaign mentioned by Mr Louis Ng, "I Quit" adopts a community-based, but personalised, approach to build a network of support to help smokers quit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Its Facebook page has more than 40,000 members, with daily exchanges by ex-smokers sharing their personal stories, smokers seeking advice on quitting and non-smokers penning words of encouragement.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We agree with Er Dr Lee Bee Wah on the need to build a conducive environment that encourages smokers to quit the habit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: HPB has been expanding its outreach and support network for smoking cessation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the past year, HPB has added over 130 new smoking cessation touch-points, including healthcare institutions and retail pharmacies, bringing the total to over 280.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These "I Quit" touch-points offer free smoking cessation counselling to smokers on the "I Quit 28-Day Countdown" programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Smokers can also call in to Quitline or access online resources for additional support to quit smoking.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, we have been educating the public on the harms of environmental tobacco smoke and its impact on loved ones, to nudge smokers to contemplate quitting.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef had expressed concern that the number of Malay smokers remained high, though there was a slight decrease in prevalence in 2013.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Please be assured that we are monitoring these trends closely.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Like Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef has pointed out, we can use culturally significant moments to nudge our fellow Singaporeans to live a healthier life.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: HPB has held the "I Quit" Ramadan roadshows since 2012.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will host another edition for the upcoming Ramadan in June 2016 and hope to encourage 2,000 Malay smokers to sign up to quit and I hope that the community will support HPB in their efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef has also asked how the amendment would be applicable to online advertising.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And Er Dr Lee Bee Wah commented that there could be limitations to the effectiveness of banning Internet advertising.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I recognise that limiting access to online advertisements is not easy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In order to effectively ban cross-border Internet advertising, there should be control at its origin in every country.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng raised concerns regarding HSA's enforcement powers under the amended Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These powers are essential to enable HSA to effectively conduct enforcement activities and investigations under the Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The amendments seek to update and, where appropriate, clarify the scope of these powers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the powers to search premises and vehicles without a warrant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The same approach has been used for the Health Products Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The existing search powers are being extended to cover vehicles because there have been several cases of illegal peddling of tobacco through the use of vehicles.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also proposed that we expand the number of designated smoking points (DSPs), like the ones in her Nee Soon South constituency.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also need to better understand the impact of having such DSPs in our HDB heartlands, including their effectiveness, prior to committing to any expansion of such a programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is also imperative that we decrease exposure of non-smokers, especially youths, to the advertising effect of point-of-sale tobacco product displays.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The aim is to ultimately de-normalise tobacco use.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also need to update and streamline our regulatory framework to ensure that our enforcement efforts remain effective and robust, yet fair.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These changes are needed as part of a bigger community-wide effort towards creating a tobacco-free Singapore and we are, indeed, heartened by the support of the public received during our consultations as well as the support of Members of this House.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.30 pm until 4.45 pm.
